summary: This standards-track RFC specifies authentication protocols based on the SHA-2 hash functions for SNMPv3's User-based Security Model. It obsoletes RFC 7630, where the MIB MODULE-IDENTITY value was incorrectly specified.

eli5.summary: SNMPv3 gets stronger ways to prove a message is genuine, using newer fingerprint math.

questions: which hmac-sha-2 protocol must snmp implementations support
how long are hmac-sha-2 keys in snmp usm
subtitle: Four stronger message-authentication options for SNMPv3, built on the SHA-2 hash family instead of MD5 and SHA-1.

tldr.problem: The User-based Security Model (USM) for SNMPv3 only defined authentication protocols based on the MD5 and SHA-1 hash functions (HMAC-MD5-96 and HMAC-SHA-96).
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines four new protocols that run HMAC over SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384 or SHA-512 and truncate the result to 16, 24, 32 or 48 octets, following the same procedure as the older protocols.
tldr.outcome: Implementations MUST support the SHA-256 based protocol and SHOULD support the SHA-512 based one. The RFC also replaces RFC 7630, whose MIB MODULE-IDENTITY value was wrong.

today: RFC 7860 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2016. It obsoletes RFC 7630 and has not been obsoleted or updated by another RFC.

sections.title: Why SHA-2 for SNMPv3
sections.content:
In the SNMP architecture, the User-based Security Model (USM) is the security subsystem of an SNMP engine. RFC 3414 defines two authentication protocols for it, HMAC-MD5-96 and HMAC-SHA-96, based on the MD5 and SHA-1 hash functions.

This memo adds HMAC-SHA-2 authentication protocols that use a Hashed Message Authentication Code (HMAC) over the SHA-2 family of hash functions. The RFC calls them straightforward adaptations of the two older protocols, so most of the machinery stays the same.

It also obsoletes RFC 7630, in which the MIB MODULE-IDENTITY value was incorrectly specified.
sections.eli5: The old fingerprint recipes used older math. This RFC lets SNMPv3 use newer math for the same job, with the rest of the process staying the same.

sections.title: The Four Protocols
sections.content:
The RFC defines four protocols, each named for the truncated output size and the hash it uses: usmHMAC128SHA224AuthProtocol, usmHMAC192SHA256AuthProtocol, usmHMAC256SHA384AuthProtocol and usmHMAC384SHA512AuthProtocol. Each uses the SHA-2 hash in HMAC mode and cuts the output down to 128, 192, 256 or 384 bits.

Implementations that conform to this specification MUST support usmHMAC192SHA256AuthProtocol and SHOULD support usmHMAC384SHA512AuthProtocol. The other two, based on SHA-224 and SHA-384, are OPTIONAL.
sections.eli5: There are four sizes of fingerprint to choose from. Every device must know the medium one, and should know the biggest one. The other two are extras.

sections.title: How They Differ from HMAC-SHA-96
sections.content:
Compared with HMAC-MD5-96 and HMAC-SHA-96, three things change. The hash inside HMAC is a SHA-2 function, so the digest before truncation is 224, 256, 384 or 512 bits long.

The digest is then truncated to 16, 24, 32 or 48 octets, instead of the 12 octets used by the older protocols.

The user's secret key MUST be 28, 32, 48 or 64 octets long, derived with SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384 or SHA-512 respectively. The older protocols used keys of 16 and 20 octets.

In the processing rules, the key length is called M, the MAC length is called N and the hash function is H.
sections.eli5: The new fingerprints are longer and the secret keys are longer too, which makes them harder to fake.

sections.title: Authenticating Messages
sections.content:
To send an authenticated message, the engine first sets the msgAuthenticationParameters field to N zero octets. It then calculates the HMAC over the whole message using the secret authKey of M octets and hash H, takes the first N octets as the MAC, and puts that MAC into the field.

To receive one, the engine first checks that the received digest is N octets long, and returns an authenticationError if not. It saves the MAC, replaces the field with N zero octets and recomputes the HMAC the same way. Finally it compares the new MAC with the saved one, and returns an authenticationFailure if they do not match.
sections.eli5: The sender writes a blank stamp, computes the fingerprint with the secret key, and fills it in. The receiver blanks the stamp, makes its own fingerprint and checks that the two match.

sections.title: Key Localization and Password Keys
sections.content:
Key localization and key change for all four protocols SHALL follow RFC 3414, using the same SHA-2 hash function as the authentication protocol in use.

If keys are derived from passwords, the derivation SHOULD use the password-to-key algorithm from Appendix A.1 of RFC 3414, with MD5 replaced by the hash function H. The password is repeated to form a string of 1,048,576 octets, which is hashed to give digest1. Then digest1, the snmpEngineID and digest1 are concatenated and hashed again.
sections.eli5: A password is stretched out and mixed with the device's own name to make a secret key just for that device.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 3414 also apply. At the time of publication, the RFC says all four protocols provide a very high level of security.

Strength depends on key length, the size of the hash's internal state and the truncated MAC length. Longer keys make key guessing harder, and a larger internal state lowers the chance of forgeries based on internal collisions.

Truncation is a trade-off. A shorter MAC is easier to forge by guessing, but reveals less to an attacker choosing messages. RFC 2104 and the cited analysis allow truncation to any length not less than half the size of the internal state.

The MIB module itself defines only object identities, so it does not by itself affect the security of the Internet.
sections.eli5: Longer keys and bigger internal workings are safer. Shortening the fingerprint helps in some ways and hurts in others, so there is a limit on how short it may be.
